terms.gloss: a lictor: an attendant of a magistrate, who walked before him carrying the bundle of rods with an axe
evidence: Cic. Q. fr. 1.1.21: apud quem prīmus quiēvit līctor (Lewis & Short)

phrases.english: under whom the chief lictor had nothing to do

long-i.html: Gell. 12.3.4: prīma syllaba in “līctōre”, sīcutī in “līciō”, prōducta est et in eō verbō quod est “ligō” correpta est; he goes on to say that līctor from ligandō, like lēctor from legendō, tūtor, and strūctor, was made prōductīs quae corripiēbantur vōcālibus, with vowels lengthened that were short. He speaks of the vowel, not only of the syllable, which is heavy in any case before two consonants. Lewis & Short’s article reports it: “pronounced līctor, Gell. 12, 3, 4”. De Vaan 341, s.v. ligō, prints līctor.
